rv.q: So it's a relief and a special pleasure to report that Mayer, in a square-cornered turn from his smart-rock productions of "Spring Awakening" and "American Idiot," has joined playwright Peter Parnell to change an unworkable plot into a more-than-serviceable gender-bending framework.

Harry Connick Jr. and his castmates make magic with the melodious score, but despite an adventurous gender-switch, the problematic 1965 musical remains as over-complicated as ever in this radical rethink.
Connick — the big star on the marquee — is just not given a character or persona within which he can rest easy.
It needs more time on the couch.
Connick may have had a Tony-nominated turn in 2006's "The Pajama Game," but here he can barely carry his songs, let alone the show.

Though done up to resemble a psychedelic fun house (the sanitized, perky kind that brings to mind middle-of-the-road rock album covers from the late 1960s and early ’70s), this “Clear Day” still has the approximate fun quotient of a day in an M.R.I. machine.
The new On a Clear Day might be an overambitious mess were it not for the winning performances and luscious music.
Surely, that’s not what’s wanted for a show that sets out to entertain — and so often does exactly that.
Well, you get the picture, even if audiences may find it spotty.
While luscious, the different tones and plug-in feel make the show slightly disjointed.
Hideous to look at and hard on the ears despite star Harry Connick Jr., the Broadway revival of “On a Clear Day You Can See Forever” is dead on arrival.

tn.cat: Best Featured Actress in a Musical

cn.t: This radical reworking of the 1965 musical boasts glorious voices and stunning visuals, but critics say the reconceived plot remains as problematic and confusing as ever, leaving the show listless despite its melodious score.

sg.ra: Closest and most direct view of the stage at St. James Theatre, with the fullest sound. The standard top pick for any show here.
An elevated, full-stage view with no orchestra-level neck-craning — especially strong for shows with big staging or choreography.
A modest side angle on the stage but still close and clear — a reliable choice when center seats are sold out.
Farther from the stage than center orchestra — less up-close, but the sound still carries well.
At 1,710 seats, St. James Theatre is one of the larger Broadway houses — far side mezzanine seats sit well off-axis and a long way from the stage.

vs.sum: The St. James Theatre offers good sightlines for most seats, though the lack of a solid rake can be an issue if someone tall sits in front of you. The sound quality is generally good, but the tight legroom can be uncomfortable for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its historic and grand interior, while facilities are average with standard amenities.

acc.note: No steps from sidewalk to Orchestra. No elevator. Mezzanine up 29 steps, Balcony up 76 steps.
